No distributional guarantee is established for the actual full-response policy.

Theorem 2 is not established as written: it relies on strong, unverified assumptions about the unavailable golden reward; assumes only finite expectations while its bound requires a finite supremum norm; and derives a one-sided reward-gap bound that does not imply the claimed convergence equality.

The guarantees are quantitatively vacuous in the experimental regime. With beta=20 and rewards in [0,1], Theorem 1 contains an exp(40) factor, requiring roughly 10^19 samples even for moderate KL accuracy under favorable divergence. The paper instead illustrates beta=1, while experiments use at most n=256. Accuracy against a finite-n baseline does not empirically verify a KL theorem.

The efficiency evaluation lacks an accuracy-versus-end-to-end-latency Pareto comparison across n. The reported numbers reveal important domination cases: Qwen3 GSI at n=16 obtains 66.9% average accuracy in about 33.3 seconds, while base-model soft best-of-n at n=4 obtains 68.9% in about 20.7 seconds; similarly, Qwen2.5 GSI at n=16 is worse and slower than base soft best-of-n at n=4. At Qwen2.5 n=256, GSI is also slower end-to-end than the same-n base baseline. GPU-seconds, memory, and the cost of dedicating separate GPUs to three models are not reported.

Baseline and tuning practices are insufficiently fair. GSI's beta and threshold are selected using MATH500 evaluation results, apparently without a held-out validation set, while RSD retains a fixed threshold despite evidence that it degenerates as n grows. Relevant speculative-decoding and test-time-scaling baselines are omitted, and the SPECS comparison uses different random subsets and sample counts.

Reproducibility and statistical reporting are weak. The claimed code-availability sentence has no URL, the code-repository appendix lists only external libraries, subset identities are absent, and confidence intervals based on only three seeds are insufficiently explained. The statement that every dataset uses N=500 also conflicts with using all 272 Minerva Math examples.

Generality is limited to two generations of Qwen models, and a math-specific process reward model is applied to non-mathematical MMLU-STEM material. The displayed traces show severe reward/model failures on that domain, weakening broader conclusions.

The core likelihood-ratio correction is essentially standard sampling-importance-resampling combined with an existing soft-best-of-n lemma; the rejection threshold is heuristic. Given this limited novelty, the guarantee-method mismatch, and the unresolved evaluation issues, the submission is not competitive at the stated acceptance threshold.

Theorem 1 concerns the unthresholded distribution tilde-pi_GSI for one reasoning step, is independent of the rejection threshold, and provides neither a finite-n guarantee for Algorithm 1 nor an end-to-end response-policy guarantee.

Theorem 2 is not established as stated: its proof gives only a one-sided bound on E_target[r*]-E_GSI[r*], which does not imply the subsequently claimed convergence of the reversed difference. It assumes only finite expectations but uses ||r*||_infinity, and its strong Assumption 2 depends on the unavailable golden reward and is not empirically checked.

The theoretical bound is effectively vacuous under the experimental beta=20 because of its exp(2 beta ||r||) factor. Accuracy approaching the base-model result does not empirically verify KL convergence, and the reported chi-square estimate uses only 64 proposal samples despite potentially heavy-tailed sequence-level importance weights. Its displayed estimator also appears to omit log around pi_S.

The efficiency comparison is not based on matched latency or a joint accuracy-latency Pareto frontier. From the reported Qwen3 averages, target S-BoN at n=1 obtains 67.5 accuracy in about 13.7 seconds, dominating GSI at n=4,16,64, which obtains at most 67.0 accuracy in about 15.0-93.9 seconds. Comparing methods only at equal n therefore materially overstates practical efficiency.

Resource accounting is incomplete: GSI hosts the draft, target, and reward models on separate GPUs, but reports latency without GPU-seconds, memory, throughput under shared resources, or deployment cost.

Baseline treatment is insufficiently controlled. GSI's beta and threshold are selected through MATH500 ablations, whereas RSD uses a fixed threshold from its paper despite the authors observing that it collapses toward the draft baseline. There is no RSD threshold/Pareto sweep, no relevant speculative-decoding comparison even for n<=64, and the SPECS comparison uses non-comparable subsets while the discussion nevertheless claims consistent superiority.

The main idea is closely related to standard sampling-importance-resampling followed by a heuristic fallback; its novelty relative to classical importance sampling and recent speculative/cascaded methods is not developed adequately.

Reproducibility is presently poor: both code-availability statements contain no repository URL, and exact sampled subsets and seed details are not supplied. Several claims of consistent or significant superiority are also stronger than the reported confidence intervals support.

The finite-sample KL analysis for the no-rejection importance-resampling variant appears coherent and usefully exposes dependence on draft-target mismatch.

The experiments cover five benchmarks, two Qwen model pairs, multiple sample counts, three hardware types, and several seeds. GSI consistently improves over draft-model soft best-of-n and the implemented RSD baseline.
Acceptance-rate, temperature, threshold, latency, and qualitative-trace analyses provide helpful insight into the method's behavior. The paper is generally clear and visually polished.
weaknesses: The central expected-reward convergence claim for full GSI is mathematically unsupported. Theorem 2 proves only the one-sided inequality E_target[r*] - E_GSI[r*] <= O(1/sqrt(n)), which does not imply that the difference converges to zero. If both component samplers converge to target distribution p and A is the acceptance set, rejection GSI instead converges to g(y)=p(y)1_A(y)+p(A^c)p(y), generally not p. Consequently, its expected reward can remain separated from that of p even under Assumption 2; the argument in Remark 3 does not make the residual term vanish.

Theorem 1 applies only to the no-rejection variant, whereas the primary algorithm and empirical results use rejection. Moreover, the guarantees are for one reasoning step conditioned on a fixed history, not the complete adaptive trajectory or final-answer distribution. The paper repeatedly presents these narrower results as guarantees for GSI as a whole.

Theorem 2 uses the finite quantity ||r*||_infinity in its proof and rate despite assuming only finite expectations. Finite expectation does not imply boundedness, so the stated rate requires an additional assumption. Assumption 2 is also strong, unobservable for the golden reward, and not empirically checked.

The theoretical bound is effectively vacuous in the experimental regime because beta=20 introduces an exp(40) factor. The reported chi-square estimates use only 64 draft samples for long sequence-level likelihood ratios and cannot reliably characterize rare-tail mismatch. Downstream accuracy approaching a baseline does not empirically verify a KL guarantee.

Efficiency is not evaluated on a matched-latency or matched-compute Pareto frontier across methods. Comparisons primarily hold n fixed even though costs differ. The tables themselves show a concerning counterexample: for Qwen3, base-model soft best-of-n at n=1 obtains 67.5% average accuracy in approximately 13.7 seconds per sample, while GSI at n=4 obtains 65.2% in approximately 15.0 seconds, so the baseline dominates that GSI point. GPU-seconds are also unreported despite GSI using an additional model/GPU.

Baseline fairness is incomplete: GSI's beta and threshold are ablated and selected on MATH500, while RSD retains a fixed threshold despite exhibiting near-total acceptance. There is no acceptance-matched RSD comparison, implemented SPECS comparison, or direct speculative-decoding baseline in the same system.

Reproducibility is presently inadequate: both code-availability statements contain blank links, dataset subset identities and confidence-interval calculations are unspecified, and an implementation-only early-stopping rule is absent from Algorithm 1. Generality is further limited to two related Qwen families, one math-oriented reward model, and predominantly math/STEM benchmarks.
